defaults.permitted_development: Across West Sussex, a wraparound extension only stays within permitted development if the side and rear elements both satisfy Class A when read together. The combined footprint, leftover garden and mass at the rear corner are often what force the scheme into a full application.

rules.height_rules: Across West Sussex, single-storey wraparounds still need to stay within the usual Class A height limits, with particular care on the side return where the 3m eaves rule can bite close to a boundary. The lower the side arm reads, the safer the design usually is.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to satisfy the normal rear-extension depth rules and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound cannot borrow generosity from one side of the design to excuse excess on the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Across West Sussex, neighbour impact is usually judged at the side boundary and rear corner together. A scheme that looks acceptable in plan can still feel overbearing once those two faces are read as one mass.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof quiet and subordinate. The more the roof wraps around as one bulky form, the harder it is to argue that the work remains a modest householder addition.
rules.materials_rules: Materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the side-and-rear combination reads as one coherent addition rather than an oversized add-on.

rules.permitted_development: A wraparound only stays within permitted development if the side and rear elements both work under Class A when taken together. In Adur, corner plots and open rear aspects make a wraparound far more visible than a standard rear addition of the same size.

rules.height_rules: Single-storey wraparound elements still have to sit within the usual Class A height limits, with the side return often controlled by the 3m eaves rule near a boundary. rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to meet the normal rear-extension depth rules, and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound layout cannot borrow tolerance from one element to excuse the other.
rules.boundary_rules: A wraparound changes two boundaries at once, so the side return and the rear corner usually need to be read together rather than as separate walls. In Adur, the boundary test usually runs on two tracks at once: neighbour amenity to the rear and loss of openness at the exposed side edge.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. Joined-up roofs that create a large boxy mass around the rear corner are more likely to need permission than a clearly secondary arrangement.
rules.materials_rules: External materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the combined side-and-rear form does not look like an overgrown add-on. On exposed coastal sites, roof profile, external finish and visual impact can carry more weight than on a routine suburban plot.

restrictions.conservation_area: In a conservation area, a wraparound has to stay visually quiet at the side return and rear corner so the original form of the house still reads clearly.
restrictions.listed_building: On a listed building, a wraparound extension is usually a listed building consent matter before it is anything else.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions can still remove the usual householder fallback on selected properties or areas, so the exact designation should be checked before relying on Class A.
